paragraphs: Boosting and online learning provide different ways to think about building predictive methods through repeated decisions. This paper develops a boosting framework by exploiting a mathematical duality between them. The central contribution is a way to bring the accumulated methods and theory of online learning into the design of boosting algorithms.

The authors use this framework to develop algorithms addressing several distinct questions. These include sparse boosting, smooth-distribution boosting, and agnostic learning. Their inclusion demonstrates the intended breadth of the framework: the connection to online learning supports multiple algorithmic goals rather than supplying a solution to just one narrowly defined boosting problem.

The relationship also produces a contribution in the other direction, yielding generalizations of double-projection online learning algorithms. The paper therefore presents the duality as a productive design principle across both areas. Its stated contribution is a collection of algorithms and theoretical connections, with the shared framework explaining how seemingly separate learning questions can be approached using related tools.
neurips-2014-a-boosting-framework-on-gro.tldr: A mathematical connection between boosting and online learning provides a framework for developing algorithms across several boosting settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method by translating its sequence of optimization steps into a continuous-time mathematical model. The authors derive a second-order ordinary differential equation as a limit of the method. This gives them another way to examine the behavior of acceleration and reason about its convergence.

The differential equation is approximately equivalent to the discrete optimization scheme, making it an analytical tool rather than an exact description of every individual update. The authors use this perspective to gain insight into Nesterov’s method and derive a family of related schemes with similar convergence rates. The contribution thus extends beyond interpreting one existing algorithm.

The continuous-time interpretation also suggests restarting the accelerated method. This leads to an algorithm with a rigorous linear convergence guarantee whenever the objective is strongly convex. That condition matters: the stated linear-rate result applies to that class of objectives. Together, the results show how studying a continuous limit can guide both understanding and the construction of discrete optimization algorithms.
neurips-2014-a-differential-equation-for.tldr: A continuous-time model of Nesterov’s method yields related algorithms and motivates a restart scheme with linear convergence for strongly convex objectives.

paragraphs: Drawing a random sample and finding an optimum usually appear to be different computational tasks. This paper establishes a connection between them for continuous distributions. It shows how a sampling problem can be transformed into an optimization problem over continuous space, extending an idea already available for discrete distributions.

The construction centers on a stochastic process that the authors call the Gumbel process. They give a new way to construct this process and introduce A* sampling, an algorithm that uses A* search to find its maximum. Randomness is therefore built into the object being optimized, allowing a search procedure to perform the sampling task.

The authors analyze both correctness and convergence time. They also compare the method empirically with closely related algorithms based on adaptive rejection sampling. In those comparisons, A* sampling uses bound and likelihood evaluations more efficiently. This finding concerns the computational evaluations needed to obtain samples, supporting the practical value of the optimization-based formulation alongside its theoretical analysis.
neurips-2014-a-sampling-7e7cd53498.tldr: A* sampling turns continuous sampling into randomized optimization and empirically uses fewer bound and likelihood evaluations than closely related rejection-based methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies graph clustering through a general representation in which each pair of nodes has an observed label. Those labels can encode richer relationships than a simple indication that an edge exists. The aim is to recover underlying groups while accommodating different kinds of pairwise information within one framework.

The authors propose a tractable approach based on maximum likelihood estimation and convex optimization. They analyze it under a general generative model and establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for successful cluster recovery. These results address two complementary questions: what successful recovery requires, and what conditions are enough to make it possible.

The theory covers existing settings including planted partitions, weighted clustering, and partially observed graphs. It also applies to settings such as graphs that change over time, giving the framework a role beyond unifying earlier results. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical findings. The main significance is a common analytical and computational treatment of several forms of graph clustering.
neurips-2014-clustering-from-labels-and-.tldr: A label-based graph clustering framework combines tractable optimization with recovery conditions covering weighted, partially observed, and time-varying graphs.

paragraphs: Training very large models across multiple machines requires attention to both the learning algorithm and the system that supports it. This paper presents a third-generation parameter server framework for distributed machine learning. Its design includes two relaxations intended to balance system performance against the efficiency of the learning algorithm.

The authors also propose an optimization algorithm that takes advantage of this framework. It addresses problems that are both non-convex and non-smooth, and comes with convergence guarantees. This links the system design to an analyzed learning procedure, making the contribution about how distributed computation and optimization work together.

The evaluation examines L1-regularized logistic regression on CPUs and reconstruction independent component analysis on GPUs. These examples use 636 TB of real data, with hundreds of billions of samples and dimensions. From these large-scale studies, the authors report that the framework offers an effective and straightforward route to scaling machine learning beyond previously achieved problem and system sizes. The evidence spans two substantially different learning workloads and hardware settings.
neurips-2014-communication-efficient-dis.tldr: A parameter server framework couples distributed-system relaxations with a convergent optimization algorithm and demonstrates large-scale learning on CPU and GPU workloads.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers can be judged by different tradeoffs among correct and incorrect positive and negative predictions. This paper studies a broad family of metrics expressed as ratios of linear combinations of those four population quantities. The family includes accuracy, AM measure, F-measure, and Jaccard similarity, bringing several familiar evaluation goals into one analysis.

The authors show that optimal classifiers threshold the conditional probability of the positive class, with the threshold depending on the chosen metric. Selecting that threshold is therefore central to optimizing performance. Simple plug-in estimators suffice to construct it for linear metrics, while the more general ratio-based case requires other techniques.

The paper proposes two statistically consistent algorithms. One combines an estimated positive-class probability with threshold selection; the other builds candidate classifiers using calibrated asymmetric surrogate losses. Both modify standard approaches and are described as straightforward to implement. Benchmark comparisons examine their empirical behavior. The theoretical result explains how probability estimation or surrogate-based learning can be connected to the particular metric a practitioner wants to optimize.
neurips-2014-consistent-binary-classific.tldr: For a broad family of binary classification metrics, optimal prediction uses metric-specific probability thresholds that two proposed consistent algorithms estimate.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from one image requires combining clues about the whole scene with details in individual regions. Unlike stereo images, a single image does not supply a second view for local correspondence. It also leaves ambiguity about overall scale, so determining how depths relate can be easier than determining their absolute size.

The paper addresses this with two deep network stacks. The first looks at the entire image and produces a coarse depth prediction. The second refines that prediction locally. This division lets the method combine a broad interpretation of scene geometry with more detailed spatial information. A scale-invariant error further emphasizes depth relationships rather than overall scale.

Using the raw datasets as large training sources, the method achieves results reported as state of the art on NYU Depth and KITTI. It also captures detailed depth boundaries without requiring superpixelation. These findings support the combination of global prediction and local refinement for single-image depth estimation, while the scale-aware formulation directly addresses a stated ambiguity of the task.
neurips-2014-depth-map-prediction-from-a.tldr: Two deep networks combine global depth prediction with local refinement, achieving strong single-image depth results while accounting for scale ambiguity.

paragraphs: This paper addresses Bayesian posterior simulation when a dataset is divided among machines in a cluster. Each machine holds only its local partition, creating a need to combine information across the distributed computation. The proposed method uses Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling as the local inference procedure at every node.

Each node runs its own posterior sampler based on its data partition. The system collects moment statistics from these local posteriors and exchanges them through expectation propagation message passing. These summaries provide a way for the samplers to influence one another with low communication costs. The stated purpose of sharing moments is to enforce agreement and improve posterior estimation quality.

The authors evaluate speed and inference quality on Bayesian logistic regression and sparse linear regression with a spike-and-slab prior. These studies demonstrate the method in two regression settings. The contribution is a distributed inference design that combines local sampling with communication through posterior summaries, connecting separately processed data partitions while keeping the exchanges between machines relatively inexpensive.
neurips-2014-distributed-bayesian-poster.tldr: Distributed Bayesian samplers exchange posterior moments through expectation propagation to improve agreement and inference quality with low communication costs.

paragraphs: Finding groups in a graph becomes harder when only part of the graph is observed. This paper studies that problem for unweighted graphs using convex optimization methods associated with low-rank matrix recovery. Both proposed programs use nuclear norm minimization to recover structure from incomplete graph information.

The two programs have different scopes. One handles dense graphs. The other handles both sparse and dense graphs but needs some prior knowledge of the total cluster size. Under the Stochastic Block Model, the authors derive explicit bounds involving cluster size, sparsity, the amount of observed data, and the regularization parameter. These bounds characterize when the programs succeed or fail.

Extensive simulations support the theoretical analysis. The authors also apply their algorithm to data from an image classification task crowdsourced through Amazon Mechanical Turk, reporting substantial improvement over traditional methods such as k-means. The combination of explicit recovery bounds and empirical evaluation helps connect the optimization approach to the practical question of how much incomplete graph information can still support clustering.
neurips-2014-graph-clustering-with-missi.tldr: Two convex methods recover clusters from partially observed graphs, with explicit success and failure bounds under the Stochastic Block Model.

paragraphs: Some signals can be represented as a small collection of waveforms appearing at different times and amplitudes. Recovering that collection means identifying which waveforms are present, how strongly they contribute, and how far they are shifted in time. The paper develops a fast method for this task, motivated in part by multichannel electrophysiological recordings.

Continuous Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, or COMP, alternates between greedily choosing component waveforms and refining their amplitudes and time shifts. This resembles Orthogonal Matching Pursuit while explicitly addressing continuous translations. The translation model builds on Continuous Basis Pursuit, using a subspace chosen to capture shifted waveforms and replacing its convex optimization approach with greedy selection.

The method also works in the Fourier domain to estimate time shifts more precisely. Tests on simulated signals and neural data show improvements over Continuous Basis Pursuit in both speed and accuracy. These results support treating waveform selection and timing refinement as interacting steps, with the continuous translation model helping recover the quantities of interest from an aggregate signal.
neurips-2014-inferring-sparse-representa.tldr: COMP alternates greedy waveform selection with continuous timing and amplitude refinement, improving speed and accuracy over Continuous Basis Pursuit in the reported tests.

paragraphs: Learned representations can allow related inputs to share statistical information, but output labels are often still treated as separate discrete objects. This paper brings representation learning to the output side of structured prediction. Its premise is that labels can have related meanings, and the model should be able to use those relationships.

The authors represent individual labels as dense vectors, allowing semantically similar labels to share parameters. They then compose label representations into larger structures using tensor products. This provides a generalization of standard structured prediction methods in which the representation of the output is itself part of what the system learns.

A joint objective learns both the model parameters and the label vectors, with an alternating minimization algorithm handling the optimization. Experiments on multiclass document classification and part-of-speech tagging outperform structural SVM baselines. The reported findings support the usefulness of learning relationships among outputs in these tasks, connecting shared label representations to better predictions rather than leaving output categories entirely independent.
neurips-2014-learning-distributed-repres.tldr: Learning dense label vectors and composing them into structured outputs enables parameter sharing and improves over structural SVM baselines on two tasks.

paragraphs: When decisions reveal only partial feedback, an action has two roles: earning reward now and teaching the decision-maker what to choose later. This paper introduces information-directed sampling to balance those roles. The algorithm explicitly relates the expected cost of a decision to the information its observation could provide about the optimal action.

It selects actions through a sampling rule that minimizes a ratio: squared expected single-period regret divided by information gain. Information gain is measured by mutual information between the optimal action and the next observation. The authors establish an expected regret bound across a broad class of models that scales with the entropy of the optimal-action distribution.

Simulations on Bernoulli and linear bandits show better performance than upper confidence bound methods, Thompson sampling, and knowledge gradient. Simple analytical examples also show that its way of valuing information can produce dramatic improvements over upper confidence bound algorithms and Thompson sampling. These are demonstrated advantages in the studied settings, illustrating why information specifically about the best action can matter.
neurips-2014-learning-to-optimize-via-in.tldr: Information-directed sampling balances immediate regret against information about the best action, with broad regret guarantees and strong results in studied bandit settings.

paragraphs: Large regression and classification datasets often need to be stored and processed across multiple machines. When there are many features, an effective distributed method must coordinate both feature selection and coefficient estimation. This paper proposes the message algorithm to do so while keeping communication between machines very small.

Each data subset first undergoes feature selection independently, using Lasso or another method. The algorithm then calculates a median feature inclusion index to combine those selections. With the selected features established, each subset produces coefficient estimates in parallel, and the final step averages those estimates. The procedure separates agreement about which features to use from aggregation of their fitted coefficients.

The authors establish model selection consistency and coefficient estimation efficiency, supplying theoretical support for the two main estimation tasks. They also report extensive experiments with strong results relative to usual competitors in variable selection, estimation, prediction, and computation time. The method is described as scaling efficiently with both sample count and feature count, making its simple coordination scheme central to its practical appeal.
neurips-2014-median-selection-subset-agg.tldr: The message algorithm combines parallel feature selection through median inclusion decisions, then averages parallel coefficient estimates with minimal communication.

paragraphs: Spatially distributed measurements can depend on one another through processes unfolding at several spatial and temporal scales. Diffusion and convection or advection contribute to this complexity in fields such as geophysics and atmospheric science. This paper studies how to learn the dependency structure behind such observations from data.

The authors show that time-series graphical models based on vector autoregressive processes capture this multiscale structure inefficiently. They introduce a hierarchical graphical model with priors derived from physics to better represent these dynamics. The hierarchy and physically informed assumptions make the model’s structure responsive to the kind of process being studied.

The paper also develops efficient algorithms for estimating interactions from observations. In a general class of exploration geophysics problems, the method discovers graph structures that have physical meaning, and the authors provide evidence of advantages over alternative approaches. The result connects statistical dependency learning with physical interpretation: the recovered relationships are evaluated as representations of a dynamical system, not solely as an abstract graph.
neurips-2014-multi-scale-graphical-model.tldr: A hierarchical graphical model with physically derived priors learns multiscale dependencies and recovers meaningful interaction structures in exploration geophysics.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many observations and how much computation are needed to estimate high-dimensional mixtures of spherical Gaussians. The authors derive an estimator using spectral reasoning, with an explicit guarantee on the L1 distance between the estimated and target distributions. Their central achievement concerns efficient use of samples as dimension grows.

For k components in d dimensions and error tolerance epsilon, the sample bound is O(d k^9 log²(d) / epsilon^4). A lower bound shows that any estimator needs at least Omega(d k / epsilon²) samples. Comparing these bounds establishes near-optimal dependence on dimension, without asserting equally tight dependence on component count or accuracy.

The computation bound is O_{k,epsilon}(d³ log^5(d)), whose hidden factor is exponential in k, though smaller than previously known. Thus, the polynomial dependence on dimension comes with a substantial component-count dependence. The paper also gives a one-dimensional estimator using roughly k / epsilon² samples up to logarithmic factors, with a separate computation bound. Together, the results distinguish sample efficiency from computational cost.
neurips-2014-near-optimal-sample-estimat.tldr: A spherical Gaussian mixture estimator achieves nearly optimal sample dependence on dimension, while its runtime retains an exponential dependence on component count.

paragraphs: Object localization can benefit from high-level information that helps interpret an image but is difficult to obtain automatically. This paper investigates how such privileged information can guide learning. The setting explicitly assumes that the extra information is available during training only, making its role one of improving the learned model.

The authors build a structured prediction algorithm based on a structural support vector machine. Privileged information enters the learning objective, and an alternating loss-augmented inference procedure handles the corresponding term. The goal is to adjust model parameters for better generalization, with particular motivation for learning reliable models from small numbers of training examples.

The method is evaluated on the Caltech-UCSD Birds 200-2011 dataset. The reported results are encouraging and suggest further investigation into privileged information for structured prediction. This is a qualified empirical conclusion: the work presents a concrete way to incorporate training-only knowledge and evidence supporting its promise. The contribution connects richer supervision during learning to an object localization model intended to operate without that extra information.
neurips-2014-object-localization-based-o.tldr: A structural SVM incorporates training-only privileged information for object localization, with encouraging results on a bird dataset.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the tension between the computational difficulty of training neural networks and the effectiveness of practical training procedures. Neural networks are known to be hard to train in general, yet practitioners successfully use stochastic gradient descent together with a range of design choices. The authors examine training complexity with that practical context in view.

The motivating choices include activation functions such as ReLU, networks larger than needed, and regularization. These practices make it useful to reconsider what existing hardness statements imply for the networks and procedures actually used. The paper frames computational efficiency as a question requiring both positive results and an account of the obstacles that remain.

The authors provide results on both sides, and some lead to new training algorithms described as provably efficient and practical. The significance lies in connecting complexity analysis to algorithm design: an analysis of difficulty also yields constructive ways to train networks. The stated findings support progress in particular settings while retaining the distinction between general training hardness and the possibility of efficient methods.
neurips-2014-on-the-computational-effici.tldr: Reexamining neural-network training complexity in light of modern practice yields both hardness results and new provably efficient training algorithms.

paragraphs: Some prediction objectives assess a collection of predictions together, rather than assigning an independent loss to each example. Metrics such as precision@k and F-measure offer useful control over prediction behavior but complicate incremental learning. This paper develops an online learning framework for these non-decomposable losses and uses it to build scalable batch solvers.

The framework extends existing online models for pointwise losses and supports efficient algorithms with sublinear regret and online-to-batch conversion bounds. The authors establish sublinear regret for precision@k and partial area under the ROC curve. A new structural result about ranked lists plays a role in these proofs.

They also develop stochastic gradient descent solvers and prove convergence to the empirical risk minimizer for a large family of losses satisfying a particular uniform convergence property. They establish that property for losses including precision@k, partial AUC, and F-measure. Experiments on real and benchmark data show that the method can be orders of magnitude faster than a recently proposed cutting-plane approach, connecting the theoretical framework to computational gains.
neurips-2014-online-and-stochastic-gradi.tldr: An online learning framework enables regret guarantees and scalable stochastic solvers for non-decomposable losses, with convergence under a uniform convergence condition.

paragraphs: Sensory evidence need not remain equally reliable throughout a decision. This paper studies optimal decision-making when reliability changes even within a single trial. It moves beyond the constant-reliability setting used in the previous theoretical and experimental work described by the authors, asking how the decision rule should respond to changing evidence quality.

The authors compute and characterize optimal behavior using a boundary in the decision-maker’s belief. That boundary depends on the current reliability of the evidence, but not on its past reliability. This is a specific statement about what determines the optimal boundary; it distinguishes the present quality of incoming evidence from the history of how that quality changed.

The paper also compares optimal behavior with simpler heuristics. For certain characteristics of the process governing reliability over time, those heuristics fail to match optimal performance and reduce reward rate by more than 50%. This conditional result shows that changes in evidence quality can have substantial consequences for decision strategies, making the reliability process an important part of the optimization problem.
neurips-2014-optimal-decision-making-wit.tldr: With time-varying evidence reliability, the optimal belief boundary depends on current reliability, and simpler heuristics can suffer large reward-rate losses in certain settings.

paragraphs: Selecting useful features becomes computationally demanding when classification datasets have both many examples and many candidate features. This paper proposes a parallel method inspired by group testing. Instead of organizing selection around isolated feature assessments, it constructs randomized tests on subsets of features and evaluates their relevance to the classification task.

Each test applies a scoring function to its chosen subset, and the collection of tests can run in parallel. The authors develop a general theory giving sufficient conditions for correctly identifying the true features. This is a conditional guarantee: the stated conditions establish when recovery is assured, rather than claiming success for every dataset.

Experiments include a challenging relation extraction task with redundant features and millions of samples, where the authors report superior performance. Comparisons across other datasets show competitive running time and accuracy against established selection methods. The method also substantially speeds up most other existing approaches when used as preprocessing. These findings give the randomized tests two practical roles: selecting features directly and reducing the work required by subsequent selection procedures.
neurips-2014-parallel-feature-selection-.tldr: Randomized parallel tests of feature subsets enable scalable feature selection, with sufficient recovery conditions and competitive empirical speed and accuracy.

paragraphs: For some statistical estimation problems, evaluating the objective or its gradient is itself expensive. This paper focuses on L1-regularized M-estimators with that property. A motivating example is maximum likelihood learning for conditional random fields, where each gradient computation requires an expensive inference step for a structured prediction model.

The authors propose a carefully constructed proximal quasi-Newton algorithm with aggressive active set selection. The approach combines the treatment of L1 regularization with a strategy for choosing which variables to work on. Its design targets the cost of optimization in settings where repeated function and gradient evaluations are a substantial burden.

A central theoretical result establishes superlinear convergence even without full strong convexity, using a restricted form of strong convexity instead. That restricted property is important to the guarantee; the result does not remove curvature requirements altogether. Experiments on sequence labeling and hierarchical classification show considerably faster convergence than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The work therefore combines an analyzed convergence advantage with empirical gains on expensive structured learning problems.
neurips-2014-proximal-quasi-newton-for-c.tldr: A proximal quasi-Newton method accelerates expensive L1-regularized estimation and achieves superlinear convergence using a restricted strong-convexity property.

paragraphs: Assigning a semantic label to every pixel can benefit from information elsewhere in the image. This paper proposes a deep feed-forward architecture called the recursive context propagation network, or rCPN. Its purpose is to enrich local visual information with an interpretation of the entire scene before producing pixel-wise labels.

The network first maps local visual features into a semantic space. It then aggregates those features from the bottom up into a global image representation. A top-down pass sends the aggregated information back to local features. Through these two directions of propagation, information from every image location reaches every other location.

Experiments on Stanford Background and SIFT Flow outperform previous approaches, with reported speed improvements of orders of magnitude. For a 256-by-256 image, GPU labeling from raw RGB values takes 0.07 seconds when a superpixel mask is already available. Producing that mask adds 0.3 seconds with the off-the-shelf implementation used. The timing distinction matters when interpreting the speed of the full procedure, while the accuracy results support the value of scene-wide context.
neurips-2014-recursive-context-propagati.tldr: rCPN distributes global image context back to local features, improving scene labeling accuracy and speed in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper introduces SAGA, an incremental gradient method for optimization. It belongs to the same broad line of work as SAG, SDCA, MISO, and SVRG. The authors aim to combine fast convergence with support for a wider range of objective functions, so that the method’s usefulness is not tied to a single restrictive problem form.

SAGA improves the theoretical convergence rates associated with SAG and SVRG. It also supports composite objectives, where a proximal operator handles the regularizer. This allows the optimization procedure to treat the regularization component explicitly within its updates, extending the range of learning objectives covered by the method.

Unlike SDCA, SAGA directly supports problems that are not strongly convex, while adapting to strong convexity when it is present. That combination matters because the same method can accommodate objectives lacking that property and benefit from it when available. Experimental results demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines stronger convergence theory, broader objective support, and empirical evidence for a practical incremental optimization algorithm.
neurips-2014-saga-a-fast-incremental-gra.tldr: SAGA improves incremental-gradient convergence theory while supporting proximal regularization and objectives without strong convexity.

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit problem, a decision-maker repeatedly chooses among options with unknown rewards and observes a reward only for the chosen option. Learning which options are promising competes with earning rewards immediately. This paper studies that tradeoff when reward distributions can change over time, rather than remaining fixed throughout play.

The authors introduce a formulation that accommodates a broad range of temporal uncertainty while remaining mathematically tractable. The central quantity is the amount of reward variation the setting permits. This makes environmental change part of the problem’s complexity, alongside the challenge of learning from feedback available only for selected actions.

The paper fully characterizes regret complexity for the class it studies by linking allowable reward variation to the smallest achievable regret. It also establishes a connection between stochastic and adversarial bandit frameworks. The result gives a theoretical account of how changing rewards affect the best possible learning performance, replacing the fixed-distribution assumption with an explicit relationship between variation and achievable regret.
neurips-2014-stochastic-multi-armed-band.tldr: A non-stationary bandit formulation characterizes how allowable reward variation determines minimal achievable regret and connects stochastic and adversarial settings.

paragraphs: Object detection with weak labels requires learning useful visual evidence from limited supervision. This paper proposes automatically discovering configurations of visual patterns that distinguish an object class. The focus on configurations makes relationships among patterns part of the evidence used to recognize and locate objects.

The authors formulate discovery as a constrained submodular optimization problem. The resulting configurations serve two purposes in the detection process: helping correct mislocalizations and identifying informative positive and negative training examples. These roles connect pattern discovery to both where a detector places an object and which examples are useful for learning.

Together, these contributions produce results reported as state of the art for weakly supervised detection on PASCAL VOC. The findings support using discovered configurations as a source of guidance when detailed supervision is limited. The approach matters because it makes the learned visual structure useful beyond class discrimination alone, applying it to localization errors and training-example selection within the same overall detection task.
neurips-2014-weakly-supervised-discovery.tldr: Discovering discriminative visual-pattern configurations improves localization and training-example selection, yielding strong weakly supervised detection results on PASCAL VOC.
